pedagogy.summary: Children read, write and convert times between 12-hour (a.m./p.m.) and 24-hour notation, and represent them on analogue clocks. The core rules: for p.m. times 1:00-11:59, ADD 12 hours (3:45 p.m. -> 15:45); for 24-hour times from 13:00 on, SUBTRACT 12 to get the p.m. time (19:30 -> 7:30 p.m.); 24-hour times always have four digits, so a single-digit hour takes a leading zero (09:45); a new day starts at midnight 00:00 (not 24:00) and noon is 12:00. The rule must be applied ONLY to the right times — a.m. times and the 12:xx noon hour are the traps.
bestPractices: Ground the +12/-12 rule in the day: a day is 24 hours starting at midnight 00:00, and the afternoon/evening hours continue counting on past 12
Pair the same time in 12-hour and 24-hour form and ask 'what is the same, what is different?'
Stress the four-digit format with a leading zero for single-digit hours (09:45)
Handle the boundary cases explicitly: midnight = 00:00, noon = 12:00, and 12:01-12:59 p.m. stay as 12:xx
Decide first whether the time is before or after noon — only p.m. times get +12
keyRepresentations: Analogue clock for representing a converted time
The 24-hour day-line (00:00 midnight -> 12:00 noon -> back to 00:00)
commonMisconceptions: Adds 10 instead of 12 to p.m. times (6 p.m. -> '16:00')
Adds 12 to a.m. times too (10:17 a.m. -> '22:17')
Omits the leading zero for single-digit hours (6:38 a.m. -> '6:38')
When converting FROM 24-hour, subtracts 12 from 12:xx times (12:43 -> '0:43 p.m.') or subtracts 10 instead of 12, or omits a.m./p.m. on the answer

learn.summary: Learners read, write and convert times between 12-hour (a.m./p.m.) and 24-hour notation and show them on analogue clocks. Core rules: for p.m. times from 1:00 to 11:59, add 12 hours (3:45 p.m. -> 15:45); for 24-hour times from 13:00 onward, subtract 12 to get the p.m. time (19:30 -> 7:30 p.m.); 24-hour times always have four digits, so a single-digit hour takes a leading zero (09:45); a new day starts at midnight 00:00 (never 24:00) and noon is 12:00. The decisive step is deciding FIRST whether a time is before or after noon — a.m. times and the 12:xx noon hour are the traps where learners wrongly apply the rule.

activities.title: Walk the 24-hour day-line and watch the two clocks agree
feedback: If a learner reads a morning time and adds 12, point to the day-line: the marker is before noon, so for the morning hours 1 a.m. to 11 a.m. the 24-hour and 12-hour hour numbers match (apart from the leading zero) — only after the noon hour do they differ by 12. (The 12:xx a.m. midnight hour is the separate boundary case, written 00:xx.)

If a learner says midnight is 24:00, ask what the clock shows one minute before and one minute after midnight; show that a standard digital clock rolls from 23:59 to 00:00, so midnight at the start of a new day is written 00:00.

When they correctly state 'from 1 p.m. the 24-hour hour is 12 more than the p.m. hour' (with the noon hour as the exception, both reading 12), reinforce by asking them to predict the next afternoon time before moving the marker.
activities.rationale: Grounding the rule in the structure of the day — a 24-hour span starting at midnight with hours counting on past noon — turns a memorised +12/-12 into a visible relationship and directly targets the +10 error and the 24:00/0:43 boundary traps. A moving marker with paired displays makes the noon crossing observable; a hand-drawn day-line with paired written times is a concrete alternative when no interactive display is available.
sourceClaims: Year 4 pupils should 'read, write and convert time between analogue and digital 12- and 24-hour clocks'.

White Rose Y4 Time (Steps 4-5) documents the exact conversion errors: adding 10 instead of 12 to p.m. times (6 p.m. -> 16:00); adding 12 to a.m. times (10:17 a.m. -> 22:17); omitting the leading zero (06:38); writing midnight as 24:00 rather than 00:00; subtracting 12 from 12:xx times (12:43 -> 0:43 p.m.); subtracting 10 instead of 12; and omitting a.m./p.m. It teaches +12 for p.m. and grounds -12 in 'a new day starts at midnight, 00:00', using paired 12/24-hour displays, analogue clocks and conversion tables.
learnerActions: Move a marker along a day-line running from midnight 00:00 through noon 12:00 and back to midnight, watching a 12-hour (a.m./p.m.) readout and a 24-hour readout change together as the marker moves.

Stop the marker just before noon and just after: just before, both displays read 11:59 (11:59 a.m. and 11:59); at noon both read 12:00 and only the 12-hour LABEL flips from a.m. to p.m. (so it shows 12:00 p.m., not 1:00). Then move on past 1 p.m. and watch the 24-hour clock tick to 13:00 while the 12-hour resets to 1:00 p.m. — this is where the 12-of-difference first appears.
Stop at midnight and read both displays; confirm the 24-hour clock shows 00:00 (a new day starting), not 24:00, by looking at what it shows one minute before and one minute after.

For a chosen afternoon time from 1 p.m. onward, read the 12-hour value, then the 24-hour value, and state the relationship: 'from 1 p.m. the 24-hour hour is 12 more than the p.m. hour' — noting that the 12:xx noon hour is the exception, where both forms still read 12.

If a day-line is available, use its paired displays and boundary labels at 00:00 (midnight, new day) and 12:00 (noon); if not, draw the day-line on paper, mark 00:00, 12:00 and 24:00->00:00, and write both forms side by side for several times.
activities.intendedInsight: The +12 / -12 relationship is not an arbitrary rule but the afternoon and evening hours continuing to count on past 12; noon and midnight are fixed boundaries, the 12:xx noon hour still reads 12 in both forms, and the 24-hour day rolls from 23:59 straight to 00:00.

activities.title: Decide before-or-after-noon first, then convert
feedback: If a learner writes 9:45 a.m. as 21:45, stop at the first step: is this before or after noon? Morning times from 1 a.m. to 11:59 a.m. keep their hour, and a single-digit hour gains a leading zero, so 9:45 a.m. is 09:45.
If a learner writes 6 p.m. as 16:00, they added 10: count on from noon 12 -> 13 -> 14 -> 15 -> 16 -> 17 -> 18, so 6 p.m. is 18:00.
If a learner gives 12:43 as 0:43 p.m., note that 12:xx is already afternoon and stays 12:43 p.m.; only subtract 12 from 13:00 or later.
If a learner gives 19:30 as 9:30, they subtracted 10 instead of 12: 19 - 12 = 7, so it is 7:30 p.m.; if they wrote 7:30 with no label, remind them to mark a.m./p.m.
If a learner writes 6:38 instead of 06:38, remind them a 24-hour time always has four digits, so a single-digit hour takes a leading zero.
activities.rationale: A worked set covering exactly the discriminating cases (an a.m. time, the 12:xx noon hour, a midnight/noon item, and a single-digit hour) separates learners who reason 'decide before/after noon, then +/-12' from those who just +/-12 the hour. Practising the before/after-noon decision first prevents indiscriminate rule application; formatting the leading zero is rehearsed as a convention distinct from the conversion arithmetic.
sourceClaims: Children tend to treat the hour and minute of a time separately and apply whole-number reasoning to each, which is consistent with mis-applying the +12 rule to the hours alone (including to a.m. times) without reasoning about whether the time is before or after noon.

White Rose Y4 Time (Steps 4-5) documents the exact conversion errors: adding 10 instead of 12 to p.m. times (6 p.m. -> 16:00); adding 12 to a.m. times (10:17 a.m. -> 22:17); omitting the leading zero (06:38); writing midnight as 24:00 rather than 00:00; subtracting 12 from 12:xx times (12:43 -> 0:43 p.m.); subtracting 10 instead of 12; and omitting a.m./p.m. It teaches +12 for p.m. and grounds -12 in 'a new day starts at midnight, 00:00', using paired 12/24-hour displays, analogue clocks and conversion tables.
learnerActions: For each time given, first state whether it is before noon (a.m.), after noon (p.m.), or a boundary (midnight/noon), BEFORE doing any arithmetic.
Convert 3:45 p.m. to 24-hour time (expected 15:45, add 12) and 9:45 a.m. to 24-hour time (expected 09:45 — add a leading zero, do NOT add 12).
Convert 19:30 to 12-hour time (expected 7:30 p.m., subtract 12) and 12:20 to 12-hour time (expected 12:20 p.m. — stays the same, do NOT subtract).
Write midnight and noon in 24-hour time (midnight = 00:00, noon = 12:00).
Write a single-digit-hour time such as 6:38 a.m. in 24-hour form and check it has exactly four digits (06:38).
Always label a.m. or p.m. when writing a 12-hour answer.
activities.intendedInsight: Whether to add or subtract 12 depends on deciding first if the time is before or after noon; a.m. times from 1:00 to 11:59 keep their hour (single-digit hours gain a leading zero), p.m. times from 1:00 get +12, 24-hour times from 13:00 get -12, and the 12:xx noon hour, the 12:xx a.m. midnight hour (written 00:xx) and the midnight/noon boundaries are exceptions handled by inspection, not arithmetic.

activities.title: Match and build a conversion table
feedback: If a learner matches 6 p.m. to 16:00, have them count on from 12 to find the afternoon hour; 16:00 is only 4 hours past noon, i.e. 4 p.m.
If a learner matches midnight to 24:00, remind them the new day starts at 00:00 and a standard digital clock shows 00:00 at midnight, not 24:00.

When a learner explains 'the minutes are identical and only the hour changes, by 12, from 1 p.m. onward (with the 12:xx a.m. midnight hour written 00:xx)', confirm this is the key idea linking the two forms.
If a learner cannot place a converted time on the analogue clock, link the hour and minute values back to the clock hands before continuing.
activities.rationale: Pairing times across formats and asking 'what is the same, what is different?' builds the relationship rather than isolated answers, and a forced choice against a well-chosen wrong option makes the +10 and 24:00 errors into discriminating decisions. Matching and choosing confirm whether a learner can recognise correct conversions; they do not by themselves require the learner to construct conversions unaided, so pair them with the independent-conversion activity above.
sourceClaims: White Rose Y4 Time (Steps 4-5) documents the exact conversion errors: adding 10 instead of 12 to p.m. times (6 p.m. -> 16:00); adding 12 to a.m. times (10:17 a.m. -> 22:17); omitting the leading zero (06:38); writing midnight as 24:00 rather than 00:00; subtracting 12 from 12:xx times (12:43 -> 0:43 p.m.); subtracting 10 instead of 12; and omitting a.m./p.m. It teaches +12 for p.m. and grounds -12 in 'a new day starts at midnight, 00:00', using paired 12/24-hour displays, analogue clocks and conversion tables.
Year 4 pupils should 'read, write and convert time between analogue and digital 12- and 24-hour clocks'.
learnerActions: Match a mixed set of 12-hour times (with a.m./p.m.) to their 24-hour equivalents, including at least one morning time, one 12:xx p.m. time, and a midnight item.
Build or complete a two-column table pairing each 12-hour time with its 24-hour form, filling the missing cell in whichever direction is blank.

For a pair you matched, state in words what is the same and what is different between the two forms (same minutes; hour differs by 12 from 1 p.m. onward and in the 12:xx a.m. midnight hour, which is written 00:xx; 24-hour has four digits).

Choose correctly between a tempting wrong answer and the right one, e.g. for '6 p.m. in 24-hour time' decide between 16:00 (a +10 slip) and 18:00, and for midnight decide between 24:00 and 00:00, explaining why the wrong one is wrong.
Represent one converted time on an analogue clock to connect the notation to the clock face.
activities.intendedInsight: Seeing the two notations paired across many times — and articulating what stays the same (minutes) and what changes (the hour, from 1 p.m. onward, plus the 12:xx a.m. midnight hour becoming 00:xx) — consolidates the rule and exposes the specific slips (+10, adding 12 to a.m., 24:00, dropping a.m./p.m.).

activities.title: Timetable word problems that force the right decision
feedback: If a learner converts a morning timetable time by adding 12, return to the before/after-noon check before the arithmetic.
If a learner gives a 24-hour timetable time back in 12-hour form without a.m./p.m., ask which part of the day it is so the label is included.
Praise answers that state the before/after-noon decision and the reason for adding, subtracting or leaving the hour unchanged, not just the final number.
activities.rationale: Embedding conversions in timetable contexts rehearses the skill where it is actually used and keeps the decision explicit. Word problems can practise and check application but do not let a learner watch the conversion method unfold step by step, so they complement rather than replace the day-line and independent-conversion work.
sourceClaims: Year 4 pupils should 'read, write and convert time between analogue and digital 12- and 24-hour clocks'.
learnerActions: Read short timetable or schedule problems (e.g. a train leaves at 15:45 — what time is that in the afternoon? A film starts at 9:45 a.m. — write its 24-hour time) and convert as needed to answer.
For each problem, say whether the time is before or after noon before converting, then give the answer in the format the question asks for, labelling a.m./p.m. when giving 12-hour times.
Include at least one morning time, one noon-hour (12:xx) time, and one midnight/noon reference so the morning and noon traps appear in context.
Explain your answer to a partner or in writing, justifying why you added, subtracted, or left the hour unchanged.
activities.intendedInsight: The conversion rule is applied to solve real timetable questions, and the before/after-noon check and the boundary exceptions still govern whether to add, subtract, or leave the hour alone.

constraints: Target age roughly 8-9 (Year 4); procedural measurement objective: read, write and convert between analogue and digital 12- and 24-hour clocks.

Always decide before/after noon FIRST; add 12 only to p.m. times 1:00-11:59, subtract 12 only from 24-hour times 13:00 onward. a.m. times from 1:00 to 11:59 are NOT given +12 — they keep their hour, with a leading zero only for single-digit hours (9:45 a.m. -> 09:45, but 10:15 a.m. -> 10:15); the 12:xx a.m. midnight hour is written 00:xx.

The 12:xx noon hour stays 12:xx p.m. — do not subtract 12 from it; noon is 12:00 and midnight is 00:00, never 24:00. At noon both forms read 12:00; the 24-hour ticks to 13:00 and the 12-hour resets to 1:00 p.m. only when passing 1 p.m., so the 12-of-difference begins after the noon hour, not at noon.
24-hour times always show four digits; single-digit hours take a leading zero (09:45, 06:38).
Always label a.m./p.m. on a 12-hour answer.

Matching and multiple-choice recognition confirm a learner can identify correct conversions but do not by themselves show the learner can construct conversions unaided; pair them with activities requiring the learner to produce conversions in both directions.

A static paired-clock poster can label the two formats but cannot show the marker crossing noon or the boundary behaviour; treat a drawn or printed day-line as a static scaffold and have the learner reason through the noon/midnight transitions aloud.
An interactive day-line is one helpful representation, not the only way to teach this; a hand-drawn day-line, a conversion table, and analogue-clock work are valid concrete alternatives.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research; sources were NOT re-fetched or re-verified. Activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions, and cited claims support general teaching principles, not the specific tasks.

Self-audit of arithmetic: 6 p.m. = 18:00 (count on from 12: 13,14,15,16,17,18); the +10 slip gives 16:00 which is 4 p.m. — kept 16:00 only as a labelled wrong-answer distractor, never as a correct option. 3:45 p.m. = 15:45; 9:45 a.m. = 09:45; 19:30 = 7:30 p.m.; 12:20 stays 12:20 p.m.; 12:43 stays 12:43 p.m.; midnight = 00:00; noon = 12:00. All verified consistent.

Corrected the noon-crossing description inherited from the original design note/recommendation ('crossing noon ... the 24-hour ticks on to 13:00 and the 12-hour resets to 1:00'): at noon both displays read 12:00 and only the label flips to p.m.; the 24-hour reaches 13:00 and the 12-hour resets to 1:00 p.m. one hour later. The original wording conflated the noon crossing with the 1 p.m. crossing and contradicted the lesson's own 12:xx-stays-12:xx rule.

Scoped activity[0].feedback[0] to the morning hours 1 a.m.-11 a.m. and named the 12:xx a.m. midnight hour (e.g. 12:30 a.m. = 00:30) as a separate boundary case, since the unscoped 'morning hours match' claim fails at the midnight hour. No task in these activities presents a 12:xx a.m. time; only midnight = 00:00 is exercised.

The source labels converting-notation as 'not a spatial task; 3D adds nothing'. This is a catalog-fit opinion, not an established pedagogical law; it has been omitted rather than asserted. No claim is made that any single medium is uniquely necessary.

The source framed the day-line marker as the moment the rule 'becomes something seen, not a rule to memorise' and rated it uniquely 'ideal'. This has been softened to one helpful representation among several, with a non-interactive drawn alternative provided, since the sources do not establish comparative efficacy.

probeDeeper: 'Is that time in the morning or the afternoon? So do we add 12, or not?'
'You wrote 6:38 as a 24-hour time — how many digits should a 24-hour time have?'
'12:43 in 24-hour time — is that just before or just after noon? So what is the 12-hour time?'
'If midnight is 00:00, what does the clock show one minute before? Is there ever a 24:00?' (boundary counterexample)

errorPatterns.pattern: Adds 10 instead of 12 to p.m. times (6 p.m. -> '16:00')
errorPatterns.nextMove: Ground the rule in the day-line — the afternoon continues 12, 13, 14... counting on from noon; count on from 12:00 rather than tacking on a half-remembered number.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Converts a p.m. time with a +10 error (6 p.m. -> 16:00; 3 p.m. -> 13:00)

errorPatterns.pattern: Adds 12 to a.m. times as well as p.m. (10:17 a.m. -> '22:17')
errorPatterns.nextMove: Check FIRST whether the time is before or after noon; a.m. times just gain a leading zero, only p.m. times get +12.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Applies +12 to a morning time (6 a.m. -> 18:00)

errorPatterns.pattern: Omits the leading zero for single-digit hours (6:38 a.m. -> '6:38' not '06:38')
errorPatterns.nextMove: Scaffold the 'always four digits' convention — a single-digit hour takes a zero in front (06:38); rehearse the formatting, not the conversion itself.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Writes a three-digit 24-hour time with no leading zero

errorPatterns.pattern: When converting FROM 24-hour, subtracts 12 from 12:xx times (12:43 -> '0:43 p.m.') or subtracts 10 instead of 12, or omits a.m./p.m.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Only subtract 12 from times of 13:00 or later; 12:00-12:59 are already afternoon and stay as 12:xx p.m.; always label a.m./p.m. on the 12-hour answer.
Anchor on 'a new day starts at midnight, 00:00'; the 24-hour day rolls from 23:59 to 00:00 and never shows 24:00.

responseLevels.gap: Applies +/-12 indiscriminately (to a.m. times too, or +10); no leading zero; midnight as 24:00; drops a.m./p.m.
responseLevels.full: Converts both directions reliably — adds 12 only to p.m., subtracts 12 only from 13:00 onwards, uses four-digit leading zeros, labels a.m./p.m., and handles midnight (00:00) and noon (12:00).
responseLevels.partial: Converts clear p.m. and 24-hour cases correctly, but is caught by a.m. times, the 12:xx noon hour, the leading zero, or midnight/noon.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Set conversions in BOTH directions and WATCH the method: (1) 'Write 3:45 p.m. as a 24-hour time', then 'Write 9:45 a.m. as a 24-hour time.' (2) 'Read 19:30 — what is that in 12-hour time?', then 'What about 12:20?' (3) 'How do you write midnight, and noon, in 24-hour time?' Watch whether they add exactly 12 to p.m. (but not a.m.), use a leading zero, subtract 12 only from 13:00 onwards, keep a.m./p.m. on the answer, and handle midnight and noon.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: The a.m. item (9:45 a.m.) catches a child who adds 12 to everything; the 12:20 item catches subtracting 12 from noon-hour times; the midnight/noon item catches 24:00. A child whose rule is 'decide before or after noon, then +/-12' handles all three; a child whose rule is 'just +/-12 the hours' fails exactly these.
